q-130710.name: Question 1
q-130710.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,-1).$
q-130710.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,-1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y)\text{ }j \\  & =(2x+y+2)\text{ }i+(-2y+x+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(1,-1) & =(2(1)+(-1)+2)\text{ }i+(-2(-1)+1+1)\text{ }j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,-1)}{‖∇f(1,-1)‖} & =\frac{3\,i+4\,j}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

q-129910.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy+8y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,-2).$
q-129910.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(2,-2)$, can be found by computing $∇f(2,-2).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy+8y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2xy+8y)\text{ }j \\  & =(2x-2y)\text{ }i+(2y-2x+8)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(2,-2) & =(2(2)-2(-2))\text{ }i+(2(-2)-2(2)+8)\text{ }j \\  & =8\,i\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(2,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(2,-2)}{‖∇f(2,-2)‖} & =\frac{8\,i}{\sqrt{{8}^{2}}}=i\end{aligned}
$$

q-130271.name: Question 3
q-130271.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,4).$
q-130271.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(1,4)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,4).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y})\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,j \\ ∇f(1,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}}\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{2}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,4)}{‖∇f(1,4)‖} & =\frac{\frac{1}{2}(i+j)}{‖\frac{1}{2}(i+j)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}})}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-xy)\text{ }j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-y)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-x)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(\frac{1}{2+(-1)}-(-1))\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{2+(-1)}-2)\text{ }j \\  & =2i-j\end{aligned}

$$

q-130719.name: Question 6
q-130719.problem: Consider the plane curve $2y-x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}).$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,1).$
q-130719.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot \frac{1}{2y}+1)i+(\frac{2y}{x}\cdot (-\frac{x}{2{y}^{2}})-2)j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{y}-2)j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(\frac{1}{2}+1)i+(-\frac{1}{1}-2)j \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨\frac{3}{2},-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x-2) & =\frac{3}{2}(y-1) \\ -6(x-2) & =3(y-1) \\ -2(x-2) & =y-1 \\ -2x+4 & =y-1 \\ 2x+y-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,4).$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{9})\,j \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}x\,i+\frac{1}{8}y\,j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =-\frac{2}{9}(0)\,i+\frac{1}{8}(4)\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,j \\  & =⟨0,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-0)\frac{1}{2}-(y-4)0 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-130722.name: Question 8
q-130722.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,0).$
q-130722.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y) & ={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-1.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})j \\  & =(2xy\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2x)i+({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)+2y)j \\ ∇f(1,0) & =(2(1)(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))-2(1))i+((1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(({1}^{2})(0))+2(0))j \\  & =-2\,i+j \\  & =⟨-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,0)=⟨-2,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{-2} & =\frac{y-0}{1} \\ x-1 & =-2y \\ x+2y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-71389.name: Question 9
q-71389.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)={x}^{2}+y.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(-1,0).$
q-71389.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy) & ={x}^{2}+y \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}-y)\,j \\  & =(-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-2x)\,i+(-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,0) & =(-0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-2\cdot (-1))\,i+(-(-1)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)\cdot 0)-1)\,j \\  & =2\,i-j \\  & =⟨2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,0)=⟨2,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(-1,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x+1}{2} & =-y \\ x+1 & =-2y \\ x+2y+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the plane curve cos⁡(xy)=x2+y. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (−1,0).

a
2x−y+2=0
b
x−2y+1=0
c
x+2y+1=0
d
2x+y+2=0
e
x+y+1=0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: cos⁡(xy)=x2+ycos⁡(xy)−x2−y=0

If we set f(x,y)=cos⁡(xy)−x2−y, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=0.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (−1,0) can be found by computing ∇f(−1,0).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (−1,0):

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(cos⁡(xy)−x2−y)i+∂∂y(cos⁡(xy)−x2−y)j=(−ysin⁡(xy)−2x)i+(−xsin⁡(xy)−1)j∇f(−1,0)=(−0⋅sin⁡((−1)⋅0)−2⋅(−1))i+(−(−1)⋅sin⁡((−1)⋅0)−1)j=2i−j=⟨2,−1⟩

Hence, ∇f(−1,0)=⟨2,−1⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (−1,0).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−(−1)2=y−0−1x+12=−yx+1=−2yx+2y+1=0

q-130724.name: Question 10
q-130724.problem: Consider the plane curve $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=2y-x-2.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,2).$
q-130724.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =2y-x-2 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+1)i+(\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-2)j \\ ∇f(0,2) & =(\frac{0}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}+1)i+(\frac{2}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}-2)j \\  & =i-j \\  & =⟨1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,2)=⟨1,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,2).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-2}{-1} \\ x & =2-y \\ x+y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

q-71396.name: Question 11
q-71396.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1).$
q-71396.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-1,0,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,0,1) & =2(-1)\,i+2(0)\,j+2(1)\,k \\  & =-2\,i+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-2\,i+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1).$

Question 11
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(−1,0,1).

a
−2i+j+2k
b
−2i+2k
c
−2i−j+2k
d
−2i+k
e
2i+2k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(−1,0,1) can be found by computing ∇f(−1,0,1).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(−1,0,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x2+y2+z2)i+∂∂y(x2+y2+z2)j+∂∂z(x2+y2+z2)k=2x i+2y j+2z k∇f(−1,0,1)=2(−1)i+2(0)j+2(1)k=−2i+2k

Therefore, −2i+2k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(−1,0,1).

q-71404.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$
q-71404.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,k \\  & =-\frac{y}{{z}^{2}-xy}\text{ }i+(-\frac{x}{{z}^{2}-xy}-z)\text{ }j+(\frac{2z}{{z}^{2}-xy}-y)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-2,0) & =-\frac{(-2)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}\,i+(-\frac{1}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-0)\,j+(\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-(-2))\,k \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x2exyz+y2)i+∂∂y(x2exyz+y2)j+∂∂z(x2exyz+y2)k=(2x+x2yz)exyzi+(x3zexyz+2y)j+x3yexyzk∇f(1,−2,0)=(2(1)+(12)(−2)(0))e1(−2)(0)i+((13)(0)e1(−2)(0)+2(−2))j+(13)(−2)e1(−2)(0)k=2i−4j−2k

q-131115.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz},$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1).$
q-131115.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,4,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\,j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\,k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz})\,k \\  & =\frac{y}{2\sqrt{xy}}\,i+(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{xy}}+\frac{z}{2\sqrt{yz}})j+\frac{y}{2\sqrt{yz}}\,k \\ ∇f(1,4,1) & =\frac{4}{2\sqrt{1(4)}}\,i+(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1(4)}}+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4(1)}})j+\frac{4}{2\sqrt{4(1)}}\,k \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i+\frac{1}{2}\,j+k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,4,1).$

q-71397.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$
q-71397.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-2,-3,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-2,-3,1) & =(4(-2)-(-3))\,i-(-2)\,j+2(1)\,k \\  & =-5\,i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-5\,i+2\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$

q-71408.name: Question 16
q-71408.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=3$ at the point $(-1,-1,1).$
q-71408.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,-1,1) & =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\  & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}\end{aligned}

Question 16
?

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface x2+y2+z2=3 at the point (−1,−1,1).

a
x+1=y+1=z−1
b
x+1=y+1=z−1−1
c
x−1=y+1=z−1−1
d
x+1=y−1=z−1
e
x+1=y+1=z+1−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

If we set f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=3.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (−1,−1,1) can be found by computing ∇f(−1,−1,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (−1,−1,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x2+y2+z2)i+∂∂y(x2+y2+z2)j+∂∂z(x2+y2+z2)k=2x i+2y j+2z k∇f(−1,−1,1)=2(−1) i+2(−1) j+2(1) k=−2i−2j+2k=⟨−2,−2,2⟩

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0,z0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vzx−(−1)−2=y−(−1)−2=z−12x+1−2=y+1−2=z−12x+11=y+11=z−1−1x+1=y+1=z−1−1

q-71406.name: Question 17
q-71406.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz$ at the point $(1,0,1).$
q-71406.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ln⁡(x+y+z)=ln⁡(2)−xyz at the point (1,0,1).

a
r=⟨12,32,12⟩+t⟨12,0,12⟩
b
r=⟨1,0,1⟩+t⟨12,32,12⟩
c
r=⟨12,32,12⟩+t⟨1,0,1⟩
d
r=⟨1,0,1⟩+t⟨1,1,1⟩
e
r=⟨1,0,1⟩+t⟨12,0,12⟩
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side:

ln⁡(x+y+z)=ln⁡(2)−xyzln⁡(x+y+z)+xyz=ln⁡(2)

If we set f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(x+y+z)+xyz, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(2).

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (1,0,1) can be found by computing ∇f(1,0,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (1,0,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(ln⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+∂∂y(ln⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+∂∂z(ln⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k=(1x+y+z+yz) i+(1x+y+z+xz) j+(1x+y+z+xy) k∇f(1,0,1)=(11+0+1+(0)(1))i+(11+0+1+(1)(1)) j+(11+0+1+(1)(0))k=12i+32j+12k=⟨12,32,12⟩

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(1,0,1) and passes through the point (1,0,1) can be written as

r=⟨1,0,1⟩+t∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t⟨12,32,12⟩, where t∈(−∞,∞).
